heros.infro: Philaenis of Samos was apparently a Greek courtesan of the 4th or 3rd centuries B.C. who was believed to have authored a notorious manual on courtship and sex, circulated widely in the ancient world. The poet Aeschrion of Samos denied she authored the notorious work.  The manual treated the art of love systematically, including descriptions of sexual positions, aphrodisiacs, abortifacients, and cosmetics. The style is simple and the treatment summary and matter of fact.   It is one of the few technical works believed to have been written by a woman.
heros.name: Philaenis of Samos

heros.infro: Nanye-hi was a Cherokee woman of the Wolf Clan who became know in English as Nancy Ward after her marriage to Bryant Ward. She held rank in her tribe as a Ghigau, which gave her the power to spare captives. She learned weaving and raising domesticated cows from a white captive woman and revolutionized Cherokee culture. She warned whites of impending attacks for which she is recognized as a Patriot by the D.A.R. and is considered an important early pioneer woman in American for advocating for a woman's voice in politics.
heros.name: Nancy Ward

heros.infro: Cuhtahlatah was a Cherokee woman who lived during the period of the American Revolutionary War. When her husband was killed she grabbed his tomahaw and attacked the enemy. Her actions inspired her retreating people to rally and they were victorious in the fight.
heros.name: Cuhtuhlatah

heros.infro: Leif Ericson, son of Erik the Red,  was a Norse explorer who arguably was the first European to arrive in North America. He started a settlement called Vinland in present day Newfoundland, Canada. Setting off from Greenland in 1002 or 1003 Leif is first believed to have landed on Baffin Island and then Labrador. Then he arrived and wintered in Vinland. Researchers in the 1950's and 1960's identified a Norse settlement at the Northern tip of Newfoundland believed to be Leif's settlement. He spent the remaining years of his life spreading Christianity in Greenland.
heros.name: Leif Ericson

heros.infro: Al-Shahrazuri was a 13th century Kurdish physician and historian and is considered one of the great philosophers of Iran. He lived in the area of today's Iraqi Kurdistan. He is primarily known for composing a major biographical dictionary of both ancient Greek and early Muslim scholars. He also wrote a number of medical books.
heros.name: Al-Shahrazuri

heros.infro: Celebrated as the Father of Medicine, Hippocrates (460–377 B.C.) was born on the Island of Cos, traveled widely throughout classical Greece in the period of its civilization's most intellectual achievements, and died in Thessaly. He is best known for penning the Hippocratic oath, one of the basic texts of medical ethics still taken by modern medical school graduates.  Over eighty treatises have been attributed to him, however, scholars today concede some were written by others who borrowed his name and reputation. His works form ten volumes, an encyclopedia of medicine and surgery as known in his day.  Unlike most physicians of his time, Hippocrates was not superstitious and did not believe in miraculous diseases or cures. He taught that proper diet is a necessity of health, and that climate profoundly influences both the mind and body.
heros.name: Hippocrates

heros.infro: Originally a military commander for Ferdinand II of Aragon, Ignatius experienced a spiritual epiphany leading to a pilgrimage to Jerusalem, prayer, penance, and the writing of a set of spiritual exercises. He took vows in 1534 and his "Society of Jesus" was recognized by Pope Paul II as an order of the Church. By his death in 1556, Jesuits were preaching throughout Europe and in foreign missions.
heros.name: St. Ignatius Loyola

heros.infro: St. Bruno was the founder of the Carthusian Order of monks and first prior of their monastery at La Grande Chartreuse in France. The order demanded strict self-denial and separation of monks from the secular life. Pope Urban II, a former student of St. Bruno, summoned him to Rome in 1090 as a trusted advisor. Resisting the pope's wish to name him Archbishop, St. Bruno returned to solitary retreat and died in 1101. In England, the Carthusian order was wiped out during the Dissolution of the Monasteries in the 16th century.
heros.name: St. Bruno of Cologne

heros.infro: Thucidides was the greatest of ancient Greek historians and author of the History of the Peloponnesian War, which details the struggle between Athens and Sparta in the 5th century B.C..   His detailed account begins with the events which provoked the war and was the first recorded political and moral analysis of a nation’s war policies.  During the war, he was elected general. Due to his connection to the great Athenian statesman and general Miltiades, who had married the daughter of a Thracian prince,  Thucidides was given command of the fleet based at Thasos.  He failed to prevent the capture of Amphipolis by Sparta and due to this blunder,  was sentenced to exile.  His exile ended with the fall of Athens and the peace of 404 B.C.  He is thought to have perished shortly after in the troubled times following the peace.
heros.name: Thucidides

heros.infro: Younger brother of Richard the Lionheart, John often conspired against his several older brothers in his lust for power. His reign, although lengthy, was wrought with public outcry and discontent.
heros.name: John of England

heros.name: Rudolph of France
